newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling lowest to dollar since early 1994.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling lowest to dollar since early 1994.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling on Wednesday slid to its lowest value against the dollar since early 1994 as traders ignored a central bank appeal for calm on foreign exchange markets.

Commercial bank dealers said the central bank sold $15 million to shore up the shilling but it weakened further to close at a commercial mean of 67.50 from 64.25 at Tuesday's close -- a decline of 5.05 percent.

This brought the shilling's total decline against the dollar to 13.45 percent since news last Friday that the IMF had halted a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) to Kenya after a row over corruption.
The shilling closed at a commercial mean of 107 to the pound, a fall of 2.88 percent from Tuesday's close of 104.
Central Bank governor Micah Cheserem urged foreign exchange market participants to trade "in an orderly manner so that losses arising from the panic and speculative transactions would be minimised".
Commercial dealers said investors were alarmed at President Daniel arap Moi saying Kenyans would have to become self-reliant and the IMF package was insignificant compared to Kenya's economy.
The dealers said the shilling had come under renewed pressure on Tuesday because of a shortfall in expected inflows from the coffee and tea sectors, Kenya's key commodity exports.
"The shilling's still looking weak because there is a lot of speculation going on," a senior dealer from a top bank said.
"We were very heading very fast for the 70 level if it wasn't for intervention," another dealer said.
Foreign investors on Wednesday offloaded a record 400 million shillings of government treasury bonds at the Nairobi bourse before buying hard currency to repatriate their profits.
The shilling's lowest level to the dollar was 69.22 in October 1993.

On Tuesday, Moi downplayed the IMF ruling and told a rally in the tea and coffee growing regions of central Kenya that the IMF loan amounted to just $205 million, compared with Kenya's $3-billion economy.
Moi said Kenya would improve tax collection and commodity exports to meet any shortfalls arising from the IMF decision.

His cabinet urged investors to remain calm on Monday, saying Kenyan citizens should build the economy from their own meagre resources. But Kenyan executives and industrial analysts rejected the message as nonsense.

The shilling losses were expected to increase pressure on the 73-year old president, who is facing a go-slow by air traffic controllers and a national strike on Friday planned by an opposition-backed alliance pressing for political reforms.
Moi and his ruling KANU party are still widely expected to win a general election this year although the opposition has found fragile unity in their demands for constitutional reforms.
